newsitem.title: INDIA: Analysts see strong growth for India's ITC.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see strong growth for India's ITC.

text.p: Indian tobacco giant ITC is expected to report strong growth in 1997/98 (April-March) on the back of increased sales volumes after a good 1996/97, stock analysts said on Wednesday.
The firm, 31.7-percent owned by Britain's tobacco and financial group B.A.T Industries Plc, on Tuesday posted a net profit of 3.42 billion rupees ($95.6 million) against 2.61 billion in 1995/96.
"ITC's 31 percent net profit growth for 1996/97 has reinforced our view on its strong growth prospects," said Rajesh Mayani, ITC analyst at HSBC Batlivala & Karani Securities.
Despite the rise in net profit, ITC shares took a beating at the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) on Wednesday as its net profit fell short of market expectations, traders said.
In afternoon trade, ITC fell 14.50 rupees, or 3.41 percent, to 424.50 with more than 3.7 million shares traded at the BSE.
The market had been expecting a profit of up to 4.0 billion rupees, traders said.
"The stock has had a good run-up ahead of the results. So, what we are seeing now is a small correction," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the Indian associate of Goldman Sachs.
ITC shares have rocketed about 29 percent since March, as foreign funds and speculators bid the stock ahead of results.
Analysts said ITC's 1996/97 performance was mostly in line with expectations, with rise in cigarette volumes driving growth.
"Basically, there were no major surprises other than the tax provision which is slighty higher than expected," said Sujoy Misra, analyst at SSKI Securities.
India's biggest cigarette firm made a provision of 2.39 billion rupees for taxes in 1996/97 as compared to 1.91 billion in the previous year.
"Earnings growth will be volume driven, while price hikes will cover increased excise and other costs," HSBC's Mayani said in a report.
"We expect ITC to record a 25 percent earnings growth in 1997/98. This will primarily be achieved from its core cigarette business."

Mayank Khemka, research head at Calcutta-based brokerage C. Mackertich, also predicted ITC profits to grow by about 25-to-30 percent in 1997/98, but said it could take a hit depending on how the company accounts for excise claims that were under litigation.
"That is one risk which could greatly alter future profit projections," he said.
ITC has made a deposit of 3.5 billion rupees against excise claims that the firm shows as current asset but could write off, he added.
The firm has undergone a restructuring by hiving off or closing down loss-making ventures.
"We see a limitation on future growth because the restructuring exercise is more-or-less complete," said Vandana Luthra, analyst at DSP Merrill Lynch.
"There are possible liabilities under excise...these issues have to be sorted out."
($ one = 35.78 rupees)
